headline: Brent breaks $114 intraday Friday on Ansar Allah-Saudi escalation
dek: Brent crude climbed $1.30 (+1.2%) to $114.47/bbl as of 0639 GMT Friday; WTI +$1.37 (+1.4%) to $100.84. Brent on track for third straight weekly gain; highest since May.
sources: Reuters (Friday oil market report, republished via cruisin929.com Oct 22 9:05PM ET)
fault_line: Paying $6.30/gallon (US diesel) for a war that was supposed to last four weeks — who bears the cost vs who sets the risk

sections.what_happened: Brent crude climbed $1.30 (+1.2%) to $114.47/bbl as of 0639 GMT Friday; WTI +$1.37 (+1.4%) to $100.84. Brent on track for third straight weekly gain; highest since May. ING: 'Even if tensions don't re-escalate, the mere possibility is likely to keep a sizeable geopolitical risk premium embedded in prices.' Analyst Linh Tran: what matters now is extent of actual disruption and time to restore operations.
sections.what_verified: Reuters base reporting; FXStreet/ING/Ritterbusch notes; consistency with Thursday $113.17 close (Reuters) — intraday Friday move, not a conflicting figure.
sections.what_disputed: Morgan Stanley/Kpler data shows physical flows remain 'remarkably resilient' — Mideast exports ~17mb/d vs pre-war ~18mb/d (recorded in 1500-03); Trump claims record oil flow through Hormuz. The price is risk premium, not yet physical shortage.
sections.why_matters: $114 oil is not a shortage — it's a fear tax. Physical flow holds at ~17 of 18mb/d, but the market now prices a year-long war. Pocketbook-first map explainer: Yanbu + Hormuz + Bab el-Mandeb vs the pump.
sections.context: Background: UPDATE to totw-20261023-1500-03 — Brent breaks $114 intraday Friday on Ansar Allah-Saudi escalation; ING flags embedded risk premium

totw_analysis: Our read: $114 oil is not a shortage — it's a fear tax. Physical flow holds at ~17 of 18mb/d, but the market now prices a year-long war. Pocketbook-first map explainer: Yanbu + Hormuz + Bab el-Mandeb vs the pump. The fault line our audience is arguing over: Paying $6.30/gallon (US diesel) for a war that was supposed to last four weeks — who bears the cost vs who sets the risk
